skeleton:
Batbout Sliders

Moroccan · Medium · Makes 8 batbout (serves 4)

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
Batbout is the msemen's (#16) plump sibling — a soft pan-cooked bread that puffs into a hollow pocket, split and stuffed the way a pita splits but sweeter, richer, and smaller: the medina's slider. At the carts it opens like a wallet for kefta, for grilled chicken, for the leftover tagine's shredded lamb; at home it is the week's wisest bread, because one batch becomes eight pockets and the pockets become eight different meals.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

Ingredients

The first filling (the cart's kefta, worth making for the batch's first pocket)

  • the #33 kefta's quick cousin
- **Make a soft dough — softer than the batbout looks — and give it the full hour.** The pocket puffs because the dough's interior steam has nowhere to go but up: a supple, well-risen dough at a medium pan is the whole physics. A stiff dough makes flatbread; the pocket is the target. - **The bridge:** none needed — flour, water, yeast. The pan should be dry (the traditional) or wiped with the barest oil film; a wet or oily pan fries the crust before the pocket inflates.

Batbout Sliders

Prep: 30 minutes, plus 1 hour rising · Cook: 20 minutes · Total: About 1 hour 55 minutes · Makes 8 batbout (serves 4)

Ingredients

Ingredients

  • 400 g flour (half all-purpose, half fine semolina — or all flour, softer); 1 tsp instant yeast (about 4 g); 1 tbsp sugar (about 10 g); ¾ tsp salt
  • 240 ml warm water (about 240 g, approximate — the dough decides); 1 tbsp olive oil
  • A dry or barely-oiled flat pan over medium heat

The first filling (the cart's kefta, worth making for the batch's first pocket)

  • 300 g ground beef with 1 grated onion (about 100 g), 1 tsp each cumin and paprika, salt and pepper; fried in a spoon of oil 8 minutes to browned, with a handful of parsley (about 10 g) at the end — the #33 kefta's quick cousin

Instructions

  1. **Knead, rise, shape (1 hour 15 minutes).** Knead the dough's elements 8 minutes to a smooth, very soft ball; rise covered until doubled, about 1 hour. Divide into 8 balls (about 85 g each); rest 10 minutes, then roll or press each to a thick 10 cm round — batbout runs nearly a centimeter thick, far thicker than msemen's stretch. Checkpoint — the rounds should be pillowy and even — thickness matters more than width, and an uneven round puffs unevenly. Keep them covered as you work; a skinned surface seals the pocket shut.
  2. **Pan-cook to the puff (3–4 minutes a side).** Cook the rounds on the medium pan — the first side until freckled pale-gold, 3 minutes, then flip — and watch the second side: the batbout should visibly inflate, doming into a puffed pillow in the pan's heat, 2 to 3 minutes more. Press nothing; the puff is the bread's purpose. Checkpoint — a finished batbout should feel like a small balloon cooling — hollow-sounding at a tap, its dome set. If it puffs and immediately deflates, the pan ran cool; the pocket still exists inside, only less dramatic. Stack the finished breads in a cloth to keep them soft.
  3. **Split and stuff, the slider's argument.** With a knife's tip, open each batbout's pocket — the bread splits at its natural seam — and fill: the kefta first, then anything the week offers: harissa's smear (#91) on the bread's wall, salad, olives, the #20 zaalouk, a fried egg. Checkpoint — eating test: the pocket's soft, faintly sweet wall giving around the filling — the kefta's cumin heat, the parsley's green, the harissa's fire on the bread itself — one hand, complete, a meal the size of a fist. The batbout's pocket keeps the filling's moisture off your hand and in the bread, which is the whole reason the pocket exists.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
No puff, flatbreadPan too hot (crust sealed) or dough too stiffMedium heat; a very soft dough
Pocket split open at the seamOver-cooked or over-handledPull at pale gold, stack soft
Breads dry next dayUnder-covered storageThe cloth stack, always

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- The dough keeps 1 day refrigerated after its rise; cooked batbout keep 2 days in a sealed bag (split, toast, butter — the second life is a feature). The kefta keeps 2 days. - Variations: the sweet batbout (honey and the #96 amlou), the whole-wheat dough. The #16 msemen is the family's layered sibling; the #21 sliders are this bread's own street argument.
